questions.stem: The Reserve Bank of India was established under the Reserve Bank of India Act in which year, and nationalised in which year?

options.option_text: Established 1935, nationalised 1949
Established 1947, nationalised 1969
Established 1925, nationalised 1935
Established 1949, nationalised 1969

questions.explanation: RBI was established under the RBI ACT, 1934 — commenced operations on 1 April 1935 (original HQ: Calcutta; moved to Mumbai 1937). Initial paid-up capital: ₹5 crore. Based on the HILTON YOUNG COMMISSION recommendations (1926). RBI was a private shareholders' bank until NATIONALISATION on 1 January 1949 (under RBI Transfer to Public Ownership Act 1948). First Indian Governor: CD Deshmukh (3rd overall; 1943-49; later Finance Minister). First Governor: Sir Osborne Smith (1935-37 — only Governor who didn't sign any currency notes).

questions.stem: The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the RBI, constituted under the RBI Act amendment of 2016, has how many members?

options.option_text: 4 members (all from RBI)
6 members (3 from RBI + 3 external, nominated by GoI)
9 members (5 external + 4 RBI)
12 members (all appointed by President)

questions.explanation: The MPC (formed 2016 post-Urjit Patel Committee; statutory body under amended Sec 45ZB of RBI Act) has 6 members: 3 INTERNAL (RBI Governor — Chairperson ex-officio; Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy; an officer nominated by the RBI Central Board) + 3 EXTERNAL (appointed by GoI for 4-year non-renewable terms). Decisions by majority; RBI Governor has a CASTING VOTE on ties. Meets at least 4 times a year (typically 6 bi-monthly meetings). Primary objective (per Monetary Policy Framework Agreement 2016): price stability — CPI inflation TARGET of 4% ± 2%, reviewed every 5 years.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the core functions of the RBI?

options.option_text: Issuer of currency notes (except ₹1 notes, which are issued by Ministry of Finance)
Banker to the Government and to commercial banks
Regulator of the securities market
Controller of credit through monetary policy tools

questions.explanation: The SECURITIES MARKET (stocks, mutual funds, IPOs) is regulated by SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India, statutory body since 1992), NOT RBI. RBI's core functions: (1) ISSUER of currency — all notes except ₹1 (issued by Ministry of Finance, signed by Finance Secretary, not RBI Governor); (2) BANKER TO GOVERNMENT (maintains accounts of Central & State govts, manages public debt); (3) BANKER'S BANK (lender of last resort); (4) REGULATOR of banks + NBFCs + payment systems (UPI, NEFT, RTGS, IMPS through NPCI); (5) CONTROLLER OF CREDIT (monetary policy — repo, CRR, SLR); (6) FOREIGN EXCHANGE manager (under FEMA 1999); (7) DEVELOPMENTAL functions (financial inclusion, priority sector lending). Insurance: IRDAI. Pensions: PFRDA. Commodity markets: SEBI (post 2015).

questions.stem: The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) in India refers to:

options.option_text: Portion of banks' deposits kept as gold reserves
Percentage of banks' Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) to be held as cash reserves WITH THE RBI
Amount banks can borrow from the RBI overnight
Reserves banks keep in foreign currencies

questions.explanation: CRR = % of bank's Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL = deposits + borrowings less inter-bank liabilities) that it must keep as CASH RESERVES WITH THE RBI — earns NO interest. Currently ~4.5% (since May 2022). Purpose: controls liquidity; raising CRR reduces lending capacity, tightens money supply. SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio, Sec 24 of Banking Regulation Act) = different % kept as LIQUID ASSETS (G-secs, gold, approved securities) — currently ~18%; this earns interest. Banks must maintain BOTH CRR and SLR. Higher CRR/SLR = tighter monetary policy. Repo Rate = interest on short-term borrowing from RBI. Reverse Repo = interest RBI pays on overnight deposits from banks.

questions.stem: Who signs Indian currency notes of denominations ₹2 to ₹2000?

options.option_text: The President of India
The Governor of the Reserve Bank of India
The Union Finance Minister
The Finance Secretary

questions.explanation: All Indian currency notes from ₹2 up to ₹2000 are signed by the RBI GOVERNOR (currently Sanjay Malhotra, succeeding Shaktikanta Das in Dec 2024). The ₹1 NOTE — issued by the Ministry of Finance, Government of India (per Coinage Act) — bears the signature of the FINANCE SECRETARY (not the RBI Governor). Also: ₹1 note was REINTRODUCED in 2015 after being discontinued in 1994. ₹2000 notes were DEMONETISED in May 2023 (though still legal tender). Currency notes are printed at 4 presses: Nashik (RBI's Security Printing), Dewas (MP), Mysuru (KA), Salboni (WB). Coins minted at 4 mints: Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Noida.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a 'quantitative' (general) credit control tool of the RBI?

options.option_text: Margin requirements
Open Market Operations (OMO)
Consumer credit controls
Moral suasion

questions.explanation: Credit control tools fall into two categories: QUANTITATIVE (general, affect ALL credit): (1) Bank Rate; (2) Open Market Operations (OMO — RBI buys/sells G-secs to inject/absorb liquidity); (3) CRR; (4) SLR; (5) Repo & Reverse Repo; (6) MSF. QUALITATIVE (selective, target specific sectors): (1) Margin requirements (% down-payment for specific-purpose loans); (2) Moral suasion (informal persuasion — 'please lend more to priority sector'); (3) Consumer credit controls; (4) Direct action (penalties on errant banks); (5) Credit rationing (ceilings on specific sectors); (6) Publicity. OMO is the most MARKET-BASED tool, actively used in the US Fed too.

questions.stem: The RBI's 'Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS)' allows resident individuals to remit abroad up to what annual limit (as of 2024)?

options.option_text: US$ 25,000 per year
US$ 2,50,000 per financial year
US$ 10,00,000 per year
US$ 5,000 per trip only

questions.explanation: LRS (Liberalised Remittance Scheme, introduced Feb 2004) allows Indian resident individuals to freely remit up to USD 250,000 per financial year (April-March) for any permitted capital or current account transaction — studies abroad, travel, gifts, investments in foreign securities, immovable property, etc. Initial limit was $25,000 (2004) → raised progressively to $250,000 (2015). TCS (Tax Collected at Source) rules apply: 20% TCS on most LRS remittances > ₹7 lakh (effective Oct 2023) — except medical, education. Not available to HUFs/corporates/partnership firms. Can't be used for trading in forex abroad, lottery, margin trading, or sending funds to FATF-flagged countries.

questions.stem: RBI's 'Payments Vision 2025' is built around FIVE anchor goals. Which among the following is NOT one of them?

options.option_text: Integrity
Inclusion
Infrastructure
Innovation

questions.explanation: Payments Vision 2025 (released June 2022) articulates RBI's roadmap with FIVE 'I' anchors: (1) INTEGRITY; (2) INCLUSION; (3) INNOVATION; (4) INSTITUTIONALISATION; (5) INTERNATIONALISATION. 'Infrastructure' is NOT one of the five (it is part of the foundation but not a named anchor). Key targets: triple digital payments, raise the number of digital payment transactions from ~100 Cr/day to ~270 Cr/day, roll out UPI internationally, CBDC (e₹ — retail and wholesale pilot from Dec 2022), rupee-denominated global payments (via RTGS linking with other countries). Earlier iterations: Payments Vision 2018, 2021-25 mid-point review.

questions.stem: The Reserve Bank of India was brought under full government ownership through nationalisation in which year?

options.option_text: 1935 — the year RBI was originally established
1947 — the year India attained independence
1949 — the year RBI became a state-owned institution
1955 — the year State Bank of India was formed

questions.explanation: C is correct because the RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act 1948 came into force on 1 January 1949, transferring ownership to the Government of India. RBI was privately owned since its founding in 1935. A common mistake is confusing the establishment year (1935) with the nationalisation year (1949).

questions.stem: The Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requires commercial banks to maintain a minimum portion of their Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) in which approved form?

options.option_text: Cash deposited with the RBI as reserve balances
Foreign currency assets held in overseas accounts
Liquid assets such as government securities and gold
Credit extended to priority sector borrowers as mandated

questions.explanation: C is correct: SLR requires banks to hold approved liquid assets — government and approved securities, cash in hand, and gold — as a percentage of NDTL. Option A describes CRR (cash kept with RBI), which is a common confusion. SLR assets remain with the bank itself, unlike CRR which is deposited with RBI.

questions.stem: When RBI conducts Open Market Operations (OMO) by purchasing government securities from commercial banks, what is the primary intended effect on the banking system?

options.option_text: Draining liquidity to curb inflationary pressure in credit
Injecting liquidity to ease credit availability in the economy
Strengthening the rupee by absorbing surplus dollar inflows
Widening the fiscal deficit by absorbing government securities

questions.explanation: B is correct: when RBI buys government securities, it pays banks in cash, directly increasing reserves and liquidity in the banking system, which encourages lending. Option A describes OMO sales (RBI selling securities), the opposite operation used to tighten liquidity. OMO is a key tool for liquidity management, distinct from rate-based tools.

questions.stem: NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development), established in 1982, was set up based on the recommendations of which committee?

options.option_text: Narasimham Committee on banking sector reforms (1991)
Shivaraman Committee on rural credit institutions (1979)
Rangarajan Committee on agricultural credit systems (1985)
Kelkar Committee on direct and indirect tax structure

questions.explanation: B is correct: the B. Shivaraman Committee (1979) recommended the creation of a separate apex institution for agricultural and rural credit, leading to NABARD's establishment in July 1982. Narasimham Committee (1991) is a common distractor as it is famous for banking reforms, but it post-dates NABARD's formation by nearly a decade.

questions.stem: The Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate (MCLR), introduced by RBI in April 2016 to improve monetary policy transmission, replaced which earlier benchmark lending rate system?

options.option_text: Benchmark Prime Lending Rate (BPLR) phased out in 2003
Prime Lending Rate (PLR) that operated before year 2000
Base Rate system that came into effect from July 2010
External Benchmark Rate (EBR) linked to repo rate since 2019

questions.explanation: C is correct: RBI introduced the Base Rate system in July 2010 to replace BPLR, but it was itself replaced by MCLR from April 2016 because Base Rate failed to transmit policy rate cuts quickly to borrowers. Option D (EBR) is actually the system that came after MCLR in 2019 for certain loan categories, making it a common confusion.

questions.stem: Under RBI's Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework for scheduled commercial banks, which of the following is NOT a designated trigger parameter for supervisory restrictions?

options.option_text: Capital Adequacy Ratio (CRAR) falling below the required threshold
Net Non-Performing Assets ratio breaching the prescribed ceiling
Return on Assets turning negative for consecutive accounting years
Loan-to-Deposit Ratio exceeding the sector-wide average limit

questions.explanation: D is correct: The three PCA trigger parameters under RBI's revised framework (2021) are Capital (CRAR/CET1), Asset Quality (Net NPA ratio), and Profitability (Return on Assets). Loan-to-Deposit Ratio is not a PCA trigger, though candidates confuse it with liquidity norms. Options A, B, and C each correspond precisely to one of the three official PCA pillars.

questions.stem: The RBI's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RBI-IOS), launched in November 2021 under a 'One Nation One Ombudsman' approach, unified how many pre-existing complaint redressal schemes?

options.option_text: Two schemes — covering banks and digital payment operators
Three schemes — banking, NBFCs, and digital transactions
Four schemes including the deposit insurance grievance scheme
Five schemes spread across regional ombudsman jurisdictions

questions.explanation: B is correct: RBI-IOS 2021 merged exactly three schemes — (1) Banking Ombudsman Scheme 2006, (2) Ombudsman Scheme for Non-Banking Financial Companies 2018, and (3) Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions 2019 — into a single, centrally administered framework. Option A undercounts by excluding NBFCs. Options C and D inflate the count; no separate deposit-insurance or regional ombudsman scheme existed independently.
